working_title: The Serial Killer Who Was a Cotton Swab
alt_title: Police Hunted a Woman Who Didn't Exist
subject: 'Phantom of Heilbronn': for years police in Germany, Austria and France linked one unknown female DNA profile to about 40 crimes (six of them murders, per ISO), including the 2007 killing of police officer Michele Kiesewetter in Heilbronn; the hunt reportedly cost ~EUR 2 million. In March 2009 investigators concluded the 'phantom' did not exist: the DNA came from a woman who worked at the factory that made the cotton swabs, which were sterile but not certified free of human DNA (sterilisation kills microbes, not DNA). Bavarian police used another supplier, which is why the profile never appeared in Bavaria. The case led to ISO 18385 (2016), the first standard for DNA-free forensic consumables.
why_potential: One of the best 'twist' payoffs in true crime: the most wanted woman in Europe was a manufacturing contaminant. Object-led (swab, lab, map of crime scenes), no gore, no private suspect to name (the factory worker is NOT named). Demand for this exact case not measured, but DNA/forensics twists perform in the niche.
hook_15s: 0-2s: A cotton swab under a lab lamp; VO 'Police hunted this woman for 16 years.' 2-6s: Map of Europe fills with 40 red pins. 6-15s: 'Her DNA was at murders, burglaries, car thefts — in three countries. Nobody ever saw her. In 2009 they found out why.'
structure: Pins spread across Germany, Austria, France
Strange pattern: crimes with nothing in common; never in Bavaria
2007 Heilbronn police officer killing raises the stakes (memorial card, no detail)
Twist: the DNA was on the swabs before they were used — factory worker's DNA (worker not named)
Clue in hindsight: Bavaria used a different swab supplier
Aftermath: ISO 18385 (2016) standard for DNA-free swabs
thumbnail_concept: Single cotton swab glowing like evidence, silhouette of a woman made of DNA strands behind it; text 'SHE NEVER EXISTED'.
animation_style: Clean lab environment, macro props, 2.5D Europe map with pins, DNA-strand motion graphics, factory conveyor (generic).

notes: Factory location differs (TIME: Austria; others unspecified) — VO says 'a factory'.
Swab supplier name appears in one secondary source only — not used.
Do not name the worker. Kiesewetter case later attributed to the NSU (2011) — not re-searched this pass; say only 'the killing was later solved' after verifying, or omit.

working_title: The Queen of Crime Vanished for 11 Days
subject: On the evening of 3 Dec 1926 Agatha Christie drove away from her home in Sunningdale, Berkshire, after a quarrel with her husband Archie, who had asked for a divorce. Next morning her Morris Cowley was found abandoned above a chalk pit at Newlands Corner near Guildford, Surrey, with some of her clothes inside (National Archives police report). A huge search followed. On 14 Dec (some accounts 15 Dec) she was found at the Swan Hydropathic Hotel (now the Old Swan) in Harrogate, registered as 'Teresa Neele' — sharing the surname of her husband's lover. She never publicly explained it; theories range from amnesia to a deliberate plan.
why_potential: Celebrity + genuine unexplained mystery + no victim = fully ad-safe and broadly appealing; the hotel-register name is a perfect single strange detail. Strong comment driver (amnesia vs. revenge plot vs. publicity). Demand not measured by a captured reference.
hook_15s: 0-2s: Abandoned 1920s car on a frosty chalk hillside, headlights still on; VO 'The world's greatest mystery writer disappeared.' 2-6s: Police search map of Surrey. 6-15s: 'December 1926. Thousands searched for 11 days. When she was found, she had checked in under one very strange name.'
structure: Twist: the name in the register
thumbnail_concept: Hotel register page with a signature circled in red ink, 1920s fountain pen; text 'WRONG NAME'.
animation_style: Frosty hillside, 1920s car (low-poly), hotel lobby interior with register prop, 2.5D map of England, newspaper-style typography (neutral, not real mastheads).

notes: Removed 'Silent Pool' as car location — car was at Newlands Corner; Silent Pool dragging is disputed.
Discovery date 14 vs 15 Dec; name spelled Teresa/Theresa — use 'Neele' on screen.
Who found the car differs between sources — not stated.

alt_title: The First Fugitive Caught by Wireless
subject: London, 1910: after music-hall singer Cora Crippen ('Belle Elmore') disappeared, Dr Hawley Crippen and Ethel Le Neve fled on the SS Montrose to Canada, Le Neve disguised as a boy. On 22 July Captain Henry Kendall, recognising them, sent a wireless message via the White Star Line to Scotland Yard; Inspector Walter Dew boarded the faster SS Laurentic, overtook them, and came aboard at Father Point (Pointe-au-Pere), Quebec, disguised as a pilot to make the arrest (31 July). Often called the first criminal capture aided by wireless. Crippen was hanged on 23 Nov 1910; Le Neve was acquitted. A Michigan State University team (announced 2007; Journal of Forensic Sciences 2011) reported that the tissue used to convict him was not Cora's and was male — a claim not independently replicated.
why_potential: A chase where the detective overtakes the fugitive across the Atlantic thanks to new technology; a disguise detail; and a 2007 DNA twist that reopens the case. Ships/ocean/wireless are excellent pipeline fits. Remains in cellar must not be shown or described.
hook_15s: 0-2s: Ship's wireless key sparks in the dark; VO 'This message caught a fugitive in the middle of the ocean.' 2-6s: A 'boy' on deck whose suit doesn't fit. 6-15s: 'Summer 1910. A captain recognised two passengers — and Scotland Yard raced them across the Atlantic on a faster ship.'
structure: Disappearance of Cora Crippen (no detail of remains)
Flight on the Montrose; Le Neve disguised as a boy
Dew's faster Laurentic overtakes; arrest disguised as a pilot at Father Point
Trial: Crippen hanged, Le Neve acquitted (court record)
Twist: MSU DNA study says the evidence tissue wasn't Cora's (label: STUDY CLAIM, not replicated)
thumbnail_concept: Two ocean liners on a map, one overtaking the other, Morse dots across the sea; text 'CAUGHT BY RADIO'.
animation_style: Ocean + liner exteriors (procedural), wireless room interior, 2.5D Atlantic race map, Morse-code motion graphics.

notes: Arrest date: Montrose reached Father Point 31 July (one source says Laurentic arrived 29 July).
DNA finding: MSU 2007 announcement, peer-reviewed 2011; no independent replication found — label as STUDY CLAIM, do not say 'innocent'.

working_title: An Entire Colony Vanished — and Left One Word
subject: Roanoke colony (present-day North Carolina): the 1587 colony led by governor John White included his granddaughter Virginia Dare, the first English child born in the Americas. White sailed to England for supplies and was delayed until 1590. Landing on 18 Aug 1590, he found the houses dismantled (not destroyed), no people, 'CRO' cut into a tree and 'CROATOAN' carved into a palisade post — 'without any cross or sign of distress', the signal they had agreed on. Storms forced him back to England; the colonists' fate is unknown.
why_potential: Iconic single-word cold open, no violence, and a 'missing distress signal' clue that viewers love to debate. Highly animatable (palisade, carved post, ocean, coastline map). Mystery rather than murder — slight niche-fit penalty.
hook_15s: 0-2s: Torch light crawls over a carved wooden post: C-R-O-A-T-O-A-N. VO 'More than a hundred people vanished. They left one word.' 2-6s: Empty palisade in fog. 6-15s: '1590. Their governor came back three years late. One sign was missing — the cross they'd agreed meant danger.'
structure: White leaves for supplies; delayed until 1590
18 Aug 1590 return: houses dismantled, no people
Theories (per NPS): moved to Croatoan Island / inland / lost — labelled
Storms stop White searching; never resolved
thumbnail_concept: Carved post in fog with the word 'CROATOAN' lit by a torch; text '115 GONE'.
animation_style: Coastal forest, palisade, fog, ship arriving, 2.5D Outer Banks map with theory routes; silhouettes only, Indigenous peoples depicted respectfully or not at all (map labels).

notes: Changed '115 people' to 'more than a hundred' (exact count not re-checked).
Dismantled-not-destroyed houses and 18 Aug 1590 landing per NPS.

working_title: Caught Because of How He Wrote One Phrase
alt_title: The Unabomber's Manifesto Gave Him Away
subject: The 'Unabomber' carried out 14 attacks with 16 bombs between 1978 and 1995, killing three people and injuring 23. In September 1995 the Washington Post (with the New York Times) published his manifesto. David Kaczynski recognised his brother's prose style and ideas and, through intermediaries, alerted the FBI (early 1996). FBI agent and forensic linguist James R. Fitzgerald compared the texts; a reversed idiom at the end of paragraph 185 ('you can't eat your cake and have it too') matched earlier writing by Kaczynski. He was arrested at his Montana cabin on 3 April 1996, pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty (four life sentences) and died in 2023.
why_potential: Forensic-linguistics twist (a phrase as evidence) is clever and non-graphic; cabin + typewritten pages animate well. Constraints: domestic-terrorism topic is advertiser-sensitive; victims acknowledged on a card; brother's decision framed respectfully (he is a living public figure via his own advocacy).
hook_15s: 0-2s: Typewriter keys strike '...eat your cake and have it too'; VO 'He was caught partly because he wrote this backwards.' 2-6s: FBI case map spanning 17 years. 6-15s: 'For 17 years the FBI couldn't find him. Then newspapers printed his manifesto — and one reader recognised the voice.'
structure: A family member recognises the writing
Linguistics: the phrase and other matches
Arrest at the cabin (1996), guilty plea (1998)
thumbnail_concept: Typewritten page with the reversed idiom highlighted, small cabin silhouette in snow; text 'HIS WORDS GAVE HIM AWAY'.
animation_style: Typewriter macro, newspaper-style page (neutral, no real mastheads), snowy forest cabin, 2.5D US case map; no bomb imagery beyond abstract icons.

notes: Casualties 3 killed / 23 injured (one source says 29 — minority).
Earlier letter's publication varies (Saturday Review vs 'a magazine') — VO says 'earlier writing'.
Phrase was one clue among many; VO says 'partly'.
